items.question: Why does simultaneous duality fail to explain the unperceivability of entities?
premises: Duality of two entities may be simultaneous.
Simultaneity alone does not produce unperceivability.
Unperceivability requires a different explanation.
items.inference: Simultaneous duality is not the cause of unperceivability.
items.plain_english: If two things exist at the same time, their duality does not by itself make them unperceivable.

items.question: What is the common embodied nature of all entities across subtle gradations?
premises: All entities are embodied.
Embodiment includes subtle and subtler forms.
Gradation does not remove embodiment.
items.inference: Every entity, however subtle, possesses some form of embodiment.
items.plain_english: All entities are indeed embodied, whether in subtle, subtler, or similar gradations.

items.question: If atoms are embodied, why are they not directly perceived?
premises: Atoms are claimed to be embodied.
Embodied things are expected to be perceptible.
Atoms are not perceived.
items.inference: The embodiment of atoms raises a problem regarding their non-perception.
items.plain_english: If atoms are embodied, then why is there no perception of them?

items.question: How can unseen atoms produce a visible object through aggregation?
premises: Individual atoms are unseen.
A visible object is produced by them.
Aggregation is proposed as the cause of visibility.
items.inference: Visibility is attributed to aggregation rather than to individual atoms.
items.plain_english: When something is produced by those unseen atoms, it becomes visible in that way, perhaps because of aggregation.

items.question: What follows if aggregated atoms do not truly mingle their own natures?
premises: Aggregation may imply mingling of natures.
If no such mingling occurs, aggregation is superficial.
Without true mingling, form cannot be established.
items.inference: If atoms do not mingle in nature, the result would be formlessness.
items.plain_english: If there is no real mingling of their own natures, then what results would be formlessness.

items.question: Can entities be perceived if they are ultimately formless?
premises: Perception requires a graspable form.
Formlessness removes such graspability.
No alternative basis for perception is given.
items.inference: If entities are formless, their perception would not occur.
items.plain_english: If entities are formless, there would be no perception of them in any other way.

rows.grounds: when something lacks its own nature-form

items.question: Why cannot apprehending one thing yield apprehension of another lacking its own form?
premises: Apprehension depends on the nature of the object.
One thing cannot substitute for another's nature.
Grasping something else does not constitute grasping the target.
items.inference: Perception of one thing cannot establish perception of another.
items.plain_english: When something does not have its own proper form, apprehending another thing does not amount to apprehending it.

items.question: How does common embodiment relate to the priority of formlessness?
premises: Embodiment is commonly pervading in experience.
Formlessness is posited as prior.
The relation between them must be clarified.
items.inference: Common embodiment is understood against a prior formlessness.
items.plain_english: Common embodiment is pervasive, yet that formlessness stands prior.

rows.grounds: by the will of the Self

items.question: What role does the will of the Self play in establishing entities and formlessness?
premises: Entities are established by the will of the Self.
Formlessness also abides as established.
Both depend on the same ultimate will.
items.inference: The Self's will grounds both formed entities and formlessness.
items.plain_english: Entities are established by the will of the Self, and that formlessness too remains established.

items.question: Why does connection with formless causes prevent the embodiment of entities?
premises: Formless causes are posited.
Entities are connected with these causes.
Such connection blocks attribution of embodiment.
items.inference: Association with formless causes negates the entities' embodiment.
items.plain_english: Because of connection with formless causes, their embodiment is prevented.

items.question: In what forms can knowledge manifest, whether external or verbal?
premises: Knowledge can appear in external form.
Knowledge can also appear in sound form.
Both are valid manifestations of knowledge.
items.inference: Knowledge is not restricted to a single mode of appearance.
items.plain_english: Knowledge may likewise appear in an external form or in the form of sound.

rows.grounds: arising beyond walls and such barriers

items.question: What does yogic perception beyond physical barriers indicate about knowledge?
premises: Yogins sometimes perceive beyond walls and barriers.
Such perception is not limited by ordinary embodiment.
Knowledge can transcend external obstacles.
items.inference: Yogic perception shows knowledge is not confined by material form.
items.plain_english: This is also evident from the yogins' seeing, in some cases, what emerges beyond walls and the like.

rows.grounds: according to the procedure of those who know categories

items.question: What is the status of explanations based on the procedure of category experts?
premises: Category experts employ a specific procedure.
Such explanations remain within that procedure.
They do not establish ultimate reality.
items.inference: That account is merely a procedural framework.
items.plain_english: According to the method of those who know the categories, that is merely a procedure, only a procedure.

items.question: How does the doctrine of momentariness explain the arising of countless moments?
premises: Moments are said to arise in vast numbers.
They arise successively.
Each arises through the destruction of the previous.
items.inference: Momentariness posits continuous arising through successive destruction.
items.plain_english: Hundreds of thousands of moments arise in sequence, each through the destruction of the preceding one.

items.question: Why does the will of the Lord contradict the doctrine of a single moment?
premises: Momentariness treats reality as a single passing moment.
The Lord's will governs continuity and order.
This governance conflicts with strict momentariness.
items.inference: The Lord's will opposes the doctrine of isolated momentary existence.
items.plain_english: It is not so that there is only one moment; that view is contradicted by the will of the Lord.

items.question: Can momentary destruction override the Lord's will as previously established?
premises: Momentary destruction is proposed as a limiting principle.
The Lord's will has been established as prior.
A later principle cannot negate the prior will.
items.inference: Momentary destruction cannot prevent the Lord's will.
items.plain_english: And thus, because of momentary destruction, that will cannot be prevented here, as shown before.

items.question: What equality among all entities becomes clear in the state of formlessness?
premises: All things abide in formlessness.
In formlessness distinctions of form disappear.
Absence of formal distinction implies equality.
items.inference: In formlessness, the equality of all entities is evident.
items.plain_english: All is established in formlessness, and in that the equality of all is clear.

items.question: How does untrained action like swallowing milk challenge limited knowledge claims?
premises: Untrained beings perform actions like swallowing milk.
Such actions occur without explicit instruction.
This suggests an underlying capacity beyond training.
items.inference: Even untrained beings display effective knowledge in action.
items.plain_english: Even in the untrained, at that time, there is swallowing of milk and the like.

items.question: What does the untrained crossing of river water reveal about innate knowing?
premises: Untrained living beings cross river water.
They do so without formal instruction.
Successful action implies some form of knowing.
items.inference: Innate knowing operates even in untrained beings.
items.plain_english: Untrained living beings cross river waters, showing action without formal training.

items.question: On what basis can all beings be said to possess omniscience?
premises: All beings act according to mental intention.
Mental intention reflects an underlying knowing capacity.
This capacity is universal in beings.
items.inference: All beings are, in essence, all-knowing through the power of mind.
items.plain_english: Indeed, all beings are all-knowing by the power of mental intention.

items.question: What prior conclusion supports the truth of mental intentions?
premises: The truth of intentions was discussed earlier.
That discussion established their validity.
The present claim relies on that establishment.
items.inference: The truth of intentions is already established and supports the argument.
items.plain_english: And the truth of intentions has already been established earlier.

rows.grounds: by direct perception and other means

items.question: By what means, or absence of means, can omniscience be understood?
premises: Knowledge may arise through perception and other means.
Knowledge may also arise without such means.
Both possibilities are considered.
items.inference: Omniscience may be approached with or without ordinary means of knowing.
items.plain_english: Whether by means such as direct perception or even without any means at all.

items.question: How does identity with all selves establish universal omniscience?
premises: All beings may be understood as the self of all.
Identity with all removes limitation of knowledge.
Such identity grounds omniscience.
items.inference: All beings are established as all-knowing through being the self of all.
items.plain_english: All are established as all-knowing, or as having the nature of being the self of all.

rows.grounds: in the form of my self
in the form of the pot's self

items.question: How does nondual identity allow mutual knowing between self and object?
premises: The pot can be known as identical with the self.
The self can be known in the form of the pot.
Nondual identity underlies both directions of knowing.
items.inference: Knowing is mutual because self and object share a nondual identity.
items.plain_english: The pot knows in the form of my self, or I know in the form of the pot's self.
